summary: NASA has watched the world's fires from space since 2000, but with two different instruments. MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012) see the same fires very differently: VIIRS detects about twice as many burning areas because it catches small, cool fires. Put the two records side by side and the switch looks like fire suddenly doubling.
details:
MOTO: ONE BURNING CALENDAR FROM MODIS AND VIIRS

Project: Moto – One Burning Calendar from MODIS and VIIRS Event: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Lusaka Local Event (14–15 November 2026) Challenge: 7.9 – Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots Team: BinaryCoders Team Leader: Simon Phiri (Programmer) Team Members: Sharleen Murambiwa (Researcher), Tinashe Victor Banda (Researcher), and Matin Wondumbu (Programmer) Repository: https://github.com/HAZEL7190/NASA  Demo Presentation: docs/Moto_demo_slides.pdf Technical Summary: docs/Moto_technical_summary.pdf

Project Overview

Moto, which means fire in Nyanja, is a satellite-based wildfire monitoring and analysis system developed by Team BinaryCoders for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project addresses a major challenge in historical fire monitoring: combining fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments into one consistent record that allows accurate comparisons of fire activity across different years.

NASA has been monitoring fires from space using MODIS since 2000, while the more advanced VIIRS instrument began collecting observations in 2012. Although VIIRS provides higher spatial resolution, detecting smaller and cooler fires that MODIS may miss, this improvement creates a problem when comparing historical fire records. VIIRS can detect approximately 2.5 to 3 times as many burning areas as MODIS. Consequently, when fire monitoring changes from MODIS to VIIRS, the recorded number of fires appears to increase significantly, even when the actual level of fire activity may not have changed.

Moto addresses this problem by developing a harmonization method that learns the differences between the two satellite instruments and adjusts historical MODIS observations to make them comparable with VIIRS observations. Using this harmonized record, the system generates a continuous fire history covering up to 26 years and transforms the information into a practical burning calendar for countries, provinces and districts. The calendar identifies when fire seasons begin, when they reach their peak, when they end, and which periods experience the highest levels of fire activity.

The main goal of Moto is to help fire management authorities, forestry departments, disaster-management agencies, national parks and local communities understand their area's fire patterns so they can plan prevention activities, allocate resources and organise patrols more effectively.

The Problem Being Addressed

Fire and forestry management authorities depend on satellite observations to understand where fires occur, how frequently they happen and when fire seasons are most active. However, comparing fire activity across multiple years is difficult because NASA's historical satellite fire records are collected using different instruments with different detection capabilities.

MODIS, which operates aboard the Terra and Aqua satellites, has a spatial resolution of approximately 1 kilometre and has provided fire observations since 2000. VIIRS, which operates aboard the Suomi NPP satellite from 2012 and NOAA-20 from 2018, provides a much sharper spatial resolution of approximately 375 metres. This allows VIIRS to detect smaller and cooler fires that MODIS may not identify.

In Zambia, our analysis shows that VIIRS NOAA-20 detects approximately 2.5 to 2.9 times as many burning 5-kilometre grid squares as MODIS during the main fire season, which generally occurs between May and November. During quieter wet-season months, the difference can increase to between 3.5 and 5.6 times.

This difference creates an inconsistency in historical fire statistics. If the raw observations from both instruments are combined without adjustment, recent years may appear to have experienced a dramatic increase in fire activity simply because a more sensitive satellite instrument is being used. This makes it difficult for authorities to determine whether fire activity is genuinely increasing, decreasing or remaining stable.

Furthermore, a single national fire season does not accurately represent the different conditions experienced across provinces and districts. Some areas begin experiencing serious fire activity much earlier than others, while some continue burning well into October. Without reliable local information, fire management services may start prevention activities too late or end patrol operations before the most dangerous period has passed.

Moto was developed to solve these problems by creating a consistent historical fire record and producing location-specific burning calendars that reflect actual seasonal patterns.

How the Harmonization Method Works

Moto combines MODIS and VIIRS observations through a structured data-processing and statistical calibration method. The first step involves filtering the satellite observations to retain confident vegetation fires. For MODIS, observations with a confidence value of at least 30 are retained, while VIIRS observations are limited to nominal- and high-confidence detections. The system also filters the fire type to include vegetation fires only, using FIRMS type 0.

After filtering, observations from both satellite instruments are placed on a common geographical grid with a resolution of 0.05 degrees, representing approximately 5-kilometre squares. Instead of simply counting individual satellite detections, Moto counts the number of grid squares that experience fire activity on each fire day. This measurement is known as a cell-day.

To account for the different satellite overpass times, Moto defines a fire day as the period between 06:00 and 06:00 local solar time. This allows nighttime observations, which occur at approximately 01:30, to be associated with the afternoon of the preceding day rather than being treated as part of a separate fire day.

The next stage is calibration. Moto uses the years when both MODIS and VIIRS observations are available to calculate how much more fire activity VIIRS detects compared with MODIS. Specifically, the system uses the 2023–2025 overlap period to learn a separate VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio for each calendar month. Monthly ratios are calculated using neighbouring months to improve stability, especially in areas where fire activity is relatively low. When an individual area does not contain enough fire observations to produce a reliable ratio, the system uses the national ratio as a fallback.

Once the calibration ratios have been calculated, Moto creates a continuous historical record expressed in VIIRS-equivalent units. Where VIIRS observations are available, the system uses them directly. For earlier years where only MODIS observations are available, it multiplies the MODIS measurements by the appropriate monthly calibration ratio.

This process makes it possible to compare historical fire activity on a common measurement scale without treating the transition between satellite instruments as a real increase in fires.

The harmonized record is then used to calculate the typical annual fire pattern, identify the most critical periods of the fire season, determine the beginning and ending of each season, identify the peak burning period and analyse long-term changes in fire activity.

Moto also identifies the critical period as the shortest continuous period containing 50% of the year's recorded burning activity. The main fire season is defined as the shortest period containing 80% of annual burning activity. Weekly fire activity is classified into critical, high, moderate and low categories.

For seasonal analysis, the system determines the quietest point of the year for each area and uses it as the beginning of its fire year. This approach prevents fire seasons that cross December and January from being incorrectly divided into two separate seasons.

Finally, Moto applies the Theil-Sen statistical method to estimate long-term trends and uses the Mann-Kendall significance test to determine whether observed changes are statistically significant.

Validation and Accuracy

To determine whether the harmonization method produces reliable results, Team BinaryCoders conducted a leave-one-year-out validation test using the overlap years from 2023 to 2025. In this test, one overlap year is temporarily hidden, the calibration ratios are calculated using the remaining years, and the hidden year's MODIS observations are converted into VIIRS-equivalent measurements. The reconstructed results are then compared with the actual VIIRS observations.

For the worldwide system using VIIRS NOAA-20, the monthly calibration method achieved a year-total error of approximately 1.4%, a monthly error of 8.6% and a monthly R-squared value of 0.99. A method using one ratio for the entire year achieved a year-total error of 0.8%, a monthly error of 9.7% and an R-squared value of 0.99. Without harmonization, the year-total error increased to approximately 62%, the monthly error reached 63% and the R-squared value dropped to 0.34.

The original pipeline, which uses VIIRS Suomi NPP, also demonstrated improvements. The monthly calibration method achieved approximately 10% year-total error and 14% monthly error during the May-to-November fire season. Using one annual ratio resulted in approximately 11% year-total error and 15% monthly error, while the unharmonized method produced approximately 59% year-total error and 60% monthly error.

These results demonstrate that harmonization significantly improves the consistency of historical satellite fire observations. Although a single annual ratio performs slightly better when comparing total yearly fire activity, monthly calibration provides better results when comparing individual months. This distinction is important because fire management authorities need to know not only how much burning occurs in a year but also when the most dangerous periods occur.

The team also conducted a synthetic validation test using artificially generated data with a known two-times difference between instruments. Moto successfully learned calibration ratios ranging from 1.99 to 2.06 and reconstructed hidden observations with approximately 1% error. Without harmonization, the error was approximately 50%.

Key Findings from Zambia

Using the worldwide harmonization system, which converts MODIS observations from 2000 to 2025 into VIIRS NOAA-20-equivalent measurements, Moto identified several important patterns in Zambia's fire activity.

At the national level, the critical fire period occurs approximately between 19 July and 13 September, meaning that half of the country's annual burning activity takes place within this period. The main fire season extends from approximately 21 June to 7 October, while the typical national fire peak occurs around 31 August.

The statistical analysis found no significant long-term trend in total national fire activity, with a Mann-Kendall p-value of 0.79. This indicates that the national data do not provide sufficient statistical evidence of a consistent increase or decrease in yearly burning over the analysed period.

However, the analysis revealed substantial differences between provinces, demonstrating why one national fire calendar cannot adequately represent the entire country.

In Eastern Province, the critical fire period occurs approximately between 28 June and 21 August, with a typical peak around 10 August. This means that fire prevention activities in Eastern Province should begin as early as June.

In Muchinga Province, the critical period occurs later, approximately between 22 August and 9 October, with a typical peak around 10 September. Northern Province also experiences a later critical period, approximately between 9 August and 27 September. These findings suggest that patrol and prevention activities in Muchinga and Northern provinces should continue well into October.

Eastern Province also showed the clearest provincial decline in fire activity, with yearly burning decreasing by approximately 2% per year between 2003 and 2025. This trend was statistically significant, with a Mann-Kendall p-value below 0.001.

North-Western Province recorded the highest average annual burning activity, with approximately 58,600 VIIRS-equivalent cell-days per year. Its critical fire period occurs approximately between 6 July and 30 August.

The original Suomi NPP pipeline, covering the period from 2003 to 2025, produced similar seasonal findings. It identified a critical period from 22 July to 15 September, during which approximately half of all recorded burning activity occurs within 56 days. The main fire season extends from approximately 20 June to 6 October, containing 80% of annual burning activity.

This original analysis found no significant changes in yearly fire totals or seasonal timing. It also identified 1,289 repeat-burn hotspots. These are approximately 5-kilometre grid squares that burn in at least 95% of the analysed years and fall within the busiest 5% of locations nationally, recording at least 8.4 fire-days per year.

These findings demonstrate that fire activity is not evenly distributed across Zambia. Different provinces experience different fire seasons, and the timing of prevention activities must therefore be adapted to local conditions.

The Moto Fire Monitoring System

Moto consists of two main components that use the same harmonization and fire-season analysis methods.

The first component is the Zambia harmonization pipeline, which is a command-line data-processing system responsible for downloading, processing, harmonizing and analysing NASA satellite fire data. It supports resumable downloads with checksum verification to ensure that data can be retrieved reliably. The pipeline converts raw satellite CSV files into cell-day tables, applies the harmonization method, generates seasonal analysis tables and produces the data required by the static dashboard.

The pipeline can be operated through several commands. The download command retrieves the required satellite archives, the ingest command converts raw observations into the common grid format, and the build command performs harmonization and generates the analysis results. The all command combines ingestion and building into one operation. Its processed outputs are stored in the Data/processed directory, while the static Zambia dashboard is generated in the web directory and uses web/index.html together with web/data/moto-data.js.

The second component is the Moto Fire Monitor, a Streamlit-based web application designed to support fire monitoring and analysis in any country for which NASA FIRMS publishes data. It provides an interactive interface that allows users to select countries, explore fire locations, analyse seasonal patterns, identify high-risk areas and develop practical fire management plans.

The application is organised into several sections to make its features easier to use.

The Monitor section provides an overview of fire activity in the selected country. Its home page displays the country's twelve-month fire calendar through a visual feature known as the ember ribbon. The hotspot map page provides a three-dimensional globe showing satellite positions and fire detections, as well as an alternative flat map and a table of detected fires. The district statistics page allows users to compare fire counts and densities across provinces and districts using maps, charts and geographical drill-down features.

The Analyse section contains the main scientific analysis tools. Its burning calendar page displays the harmonized MODIS and VIIRS fire record, including critical weeks, seasonal timing, long-term trends, monthly calibration ratios and validation results. The historical trends page provides annual fire totals, statistical significance tests, seasonal heatmaps, seasonal envelopes and unusual monthly activity.

The Decide section transforms the analytical results into practical information for fire management. The decision support page provides seasonal outlooks, district risk rankings and recommended preparation and patrol periods. The action plans page allows users to record management decisions, assign responsibilities, set priorities, track progress and establish deadlines.

The Data section allows users to manage and access the satellite datasets. The data manager supports the loading of FIRMS archives, API date ranges and CSV uploads, while also providing tools to inspect and manage stored data batches. The downloads page allows users to export available results in CSV format.

The application also supports an optional account system that includes sign-in, account creation, user profiles and administration. When accounts are enabled, access control and user activity auditing are available.

Global Coverage and Additional Features

One of the important features of Moto is that it is not limited to Zambia. The application is designed to work with any country for which NASA FIRMS provides satellite fire observations.

When a user selects a country that does not yet have stored fire data, Moto can automatically download the latest available NASA yearly archive in the background. If the user has configured a NASA FIRMS MAP_KEY, the application can also retrieve the latest seven days of near-real-time VIIRS NOAA-20 fire detections.

The system includes a bulk importer that supports NASA's worldwide MODIS yearly archives covering the period from 2000 to 2025 and approximately 200 countries. This makes it possible to expand the analysis beyond Zambia and apply the same monitoring approach to other parts of the world.

Moto also uses geoBoundaries to obtain country, provincial and district administrative boundaries. These boundaries are cached locally to improve performance, and the Zambia provincial and district boundaries have already been checked into the repository.

To improve accessibility, the interface supports five languages: English, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Arabic. Arabic is supported with a right-to-left interface layout. The application also provides light and dark visual themes.

Project Architecture and Code Organization

The Moto project is built using Python and several scientific computing and geographical analysis libraries.

The main application entry point is app.py, which manages navigation, pages and the sidebar. The firecal directory contains the core data-processing and analysis package.

Within this package, config.py manages system settings, including grid resolution, filtering requirements, analysis years and file paths. download.py handles satellite data downloads, while ingest.py converts raw satellite detections into cell-day tables using the common geographical grid.

The harmonization calculations and validation procedures are implemented in harmonize.py. Seasonal analysis, critical periods, seasonal timing and statistical trends are handled by seasons.py. The build.py module combines the analysis stages and generates the harmonized calendar and static dashboard data.

The burncal.py module generates burning calendars for selected geographical areas. The firms.py module handles NASA FIRMS archives, near-real-time API data and CSV uploads, converting them into a consistent detection format.

The store.py module manages the storage of data for individual countries. It organises data using ISO3 country codes and stores processed batches in Parquet format, together with a manifest.json file that records data coverage.

The bulk.py module supports large-scale worldwide data imports, while seed.py provides default data preparation for Zambia and Kenya. The geo.py module manages geographical boundaries, including country outlines and administrative divisions.

Other analytical functions are implemented in analytics.py, which handles filters, key performance indicators, district statistics, trends, seasonal outlooks and risk rankings. The explorer.py module provides reusable components for exploring different types of data. The accounts.py module manages optional user accounts, password security, audit logs and action plans.

The ui directory contains the Streamlit interface. Its pages directory contains the individual application pages, while globe.py implements the three-dimensional globe using globe.gl and satellite.js. Other modules manage automatic data loading, application state, internationalisation, translations and the visual theme.

The web directory contains the static Zambia dashboard, while tests contains the automated testing suite. The docs directory contains the project's documentation, submission materials, technical summary and presentation slides. The Data/boundaries directory contains the checked-in Zambia administrative boundary files.

Data Sources

Moto relies primarily on open satellite fire data provided by NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System, commonly known as NASA FIRMS.

The first major data source is NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1, which provides fire observations from the Terra and Aqua satellites. These archives provide the historical fire record beginning in 2000 and are available through NASA's FIRMS country archive service.

The second major source is NASA FIRMS VIIRS data from the NOAA-20 and Suomi NPP satellites. These observations provide the higher-resolution reference measurements used to calibrate and harmonize the historical MODIS record.

For near-real-time monitoring, the application can optionally use the NASA FIRMS area API to retrieve the latest VIIRS NOAA-20 observations. This feature requires a free NASA FIRMS MAP_KEY.

The application also uses NASA Blue Marble imagery to provide geographical visualisation on the three-dimensional globe. Administrative boundaries are obtained from geoBoundaries, which provides openly licensed geographical data, mostly under Creative Commons Attribution licences. CelesTrak provides the orbital elements required to calculate and display satellite positions on the globe.

The yearly satellite archives can be downloaded without an API key. Only the optional near-real-time data retrieval feature requires a FIRMS MAP_KEY.

Installation and Running the System

Moto can be installed and run locally using Python. Users first need to create a Python virtual environment and activate it before installing the project's dependencies.

On Windows, the environment can be created and activated using the following commands:

bash

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt

On macOS or Linux, the activation command is:

bash

source .venv/bin/activate

Once the dependencies have been installed, the Moto Fire Monitor can be started by running:

bash

streamlit run app.py

The application also supports optional configuration through a .env file. Users can copy .env.example to .env and configure the required settings.

FIRMS_MAP_KEY can be added to enable near-real-time NASA fire observations. MOTO_AUTH can be set to on to enable the account system, which is disabled by default. MOTO_ADMIN_SETUP_CODE can be configured to provide a one-time code for registering the first administrator.

The system also provides commands for preparing and importing satellite data. Running python -m firecal.seed loads the default Zambia and Kenya datasets, while python -m firecal.bulk starts the bulk import of worldwide MODIS archives covering 2000 to 2025.

To run the automated tests, users can execute:

bash

python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

The project requires Python and several scientific, geographical and application-development libraries, including pandas, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj, PyArrow, requests, Streamlit, seaborn, Matplotlib, pydeck and pycountry.

Security and Quality Assurance

Security and reliability were considered during the development of Moto, particularly because the application can manage user accounts, satellite data and optional NASA API credentials.

Passwords are stored using salted PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 password hashes rather than being stored as plain text. The account system also includes protection against repeated failed sign-in attempts by temporarily locking accounts after multiple unsuccessful attempts. An audit log records relevant user activities to support accountability.

The application also protects the NASA FIRMS API key by ensuring that it is not written into downloaded CSV files or exposed through error messages.

Data quality is another important consideration. Moto only calculates baselines and trends using months for which the system has actual data coverage. This prevents missing data from being incorrectly interpreted as months with no fire activity. The system also ensures that trends are calculated using observations from one instrument at a time unless the records have been harmonized.

The project includes 105 automated tests covering the data-processing pipeline, harmonization calculations, security features, translations and application pages. During the last recorded test run, all 105 tests completed successfully, with two tests skipped.

The SECURITY.md document provides additional information about API key handling, account security and recommendations for hosting the application publicly.

Limitations of the System

Although Moto provides a more consistent approach to historical fire monitoring, there are several limitations that users should understand when interpreting its results.

Satellite instruments can only detect fires when they are burning at the time the satellite passes overhead. As a result, fires that occur between satellite overpasses may be missed. Smoke, clouds and other atmospheric conditions can also prevent satellites from detecting some fires.

Another important limitation is that Moto analyses active-fire detections rather than directly measuring the total land area burned. A high number of active-fire detections does not necessarily represent an equivalent increase in burned area.

The harmonization ratios are currently learned using three overlap years, from 2023 to 2025, and are assumed to remain applicable to earlier MODIS observations. Future work will investigate using the longer period of simultaneous satellite observations to improve calibration.

The MODIS observations from 2000 to 2002 also require special consideration because Terra was the main available source during those years, meaning that fire activity may be undercounted compared with later years when both Terra and Aqua contributed observations. For this reason, the original Suomi NPP pipeline begins in 2003.

In areas where fire activity is too low to produce reliable calibration ratios during the overlap period, Moto uses the national calibration ratio where appropriate and identifies areas that remain on the MODIS measurement scale only. This is important because users should not interpret those areas as having the same level of calibration confidence as locations with sufficient overlap data.

Finally, the available yearly satellite archives currently extend through December 2025. Monitoring fires during 2026 requires the optional near-real-time NASA FIRMS data feed.

Beneficiaries and Future Development

Moto is intended to support organizations and communities that depend on accurate information about fire activity and seasonal patterns.

The main beneficiaries include district fire and forestry officers, national forestry departments, disaster-management agencies, national parks, wildlife conservation services and farming communities. By providing reliable historical information about fire activity, Moto can help these groups identify dangerous periods, prioritize high-risk locations, prepare resources and organize prevention patrols according to local conditions.

The system is particularly valuable because it allows users to move beyond a single national fire season and understand the different seasonal patterns experienced by individual provinces and districts.

Future development will focus on improving the harmonization method by using every available overlap year, including observations from Suomi NPP beginning in 2012 and NOAA-20 beginning in 2018. This would provide a longer calibration period and help determine whether the relationship between MODIS and VIIRS has changed over time.

Another planned improvement is the comparison of near-real-time fire detections with the normal weekly burning patterns of individual districts. This could help identify unusual fire activity and provide earlier warnings to fire management authorities.

The team also intends to integrate burned-area measurements from NASA's MODIS MCD64A1 product and weather information from NASA POWER. These additional datasets would help explain not only where fires are detected but also how much land is affected and how weather conditions influence fire activity.

Finally, the team plans to strengthen the validation process by comparing satellite observations with actual fire reports collected from local fire services and other ground-based sources.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

During the development of Moto, Team BinaryCoders used Claude, developed by Anthropic and accessed through Claude Code, as a coding assistant. It supported the development of the data-processing pipeline, application features, automated tests and project documentation.

However, the team selected the NASA Space Apps Challenge, identified the problem, designed the harmonization approach, determined the research questions, executed the code using NASA satellite data and reviewed the resulting findings. The numerical results presented in the project were generated by running the developed system on NASA data.

Conclusion

Moto: One Burning Calendar from MODIS and VIIRS is designed to solve an important problem in historical satellite fire monitoring by making observations from different satellite instruments comparable over time. Through monthly calibration, a common geographical grid and statistical analysis, Moto transforms separate MODIS and VIIRS records into one continuous, harmonized fire history.

More importantly, the project converts complex satellite observations into practical information that can support real-world fire management. Its burning calendars identify critical fire periods, seasonal peaks, long-term trends and repeatedly burning hotspots at national, provincial and district levels.

The findings from Zambia demonstrate that fire seasons vary significantly between provinces and that a single national calendar cannot adequately guide every area. By identifying these local differences, Moto helps fire management authorities determine when prevention activities should begin, where patrol resources should be concentrated and how long monitoring operations should continue.

Ultimately, Moto aims to turn NASA's historical satellite fire data into a practical decision-support resource that helps communities and authorities understand fire patterns, prepare for dangerous seasons and make better-informed decisions to protect forests, wildlife, livelihoods and the environment.
